title: Rebecca Gratz
hookLine: founded the first Jewish Sunday school in America in 1838

lines: WHY NOT ONE OF OUR OWN?
cards: Sunday morning in Philadelphia. Church bells. Children in their best clothes walking to Sunday school, lesson books under their arms.
And a few Jewish children watching them go, or walking along with their friends, because there is no Jewish school for them to go to.
A woman named Rebecca Gratz notices, and asks a practical question: why not a school for Jewish children, on the day they're free? In 1838, her answer gets its first class.

teach.b: Rebecca Gratz was already busy. From a well-known Jewish family in Philadelphia, she had spent years building things for people in need: a society to help orphans, a society of Jewish women to help poor Jewish families.
She never married, and she helped raise her sister's children after their mother died.

teach.h: A SCHOOL ON THE DAY THEY'RE FREE.
teach.b: Then came the school she called the Hebrew Sunday School.
A school on Sunday was an idea her Christian neighbors already used, and she saw no reason Jewish children couldn't have it too, filled with their own Bible, their own prayers, their own history.
The teachers were young Jewish women, volunteers. They had few books, so they made do, and some wrote the lessons themselves. The children came.

Behind it is a command the Torah gives every parent, in the Shema itself: "and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thy house, and when thou walkest by the way."
Rebecca Gratz asked: and when the parents can't, who will?
The school answered: the community will, and women would teach. Her model, a weekend Jewish school run by the community, spread to other cities, and versions of it still exist in synagogues today.
People also tell a story that she was the model for the Jewish heroine Rebecca in Walter Scott's novel Ivanhoe. Nobody has proven it.
What can be shown is quieter: a woman, a free morning, and children who learned their own story.

how: Synagogues in America run weekend or after-school religious schools where volunteer and part-time teachers teach Hebrew, prayer, Bible, holidays and history, a model often traced to Rebecca Gratz's Hebrew Sunday School in Philadelphia.

games.q: you're Rebecca Gratz. Jewish children in your city have no Jewish school, and their Christian friends go to Sunday school. what do you do?
o: send them to the church schools.
start a Jewish school on the day they're free.
wait for the synagogue to do it.
games.why: she opened the Hebrew Sunday School, borrowing the day and the idea from her neighbors and filling it with the children's own Bible, prayers and history.

practice: Hold a child in your life in mind, your own, a relative, a neighbor, a student, and one small thing you know that they don't yet: how to tie a knot, a family story, a blessing, why the moon changes shape.
Picture telling them, where you'd sit and what they'd ask. If you pray, you can hold that child in your prayer; if not, simply hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Rebecca Gratz. The Philadelphia woman who built help for orphans and the poor, and opened the Hebrew Sunday School so Jewish children could learn their own story. Today's word.
